frase_gancho.texto: A relief that may record an eclipse and the correction of a calendar.

puente_narrativo.texto: Follow your route: the writing of the city has more to say about these dates.

guion_corto.texto: This pyramid can also be read as a record of the sky. According to the INAH guide, on the west façade there is an image related to the adjustment of the calendar, beside the name and rank of a ruler. Another relief shows a jaw about to swallow a circle divided into four. Medina Romero interprets it as the Moon covering the Sun. He proposes an eclipse in the year seven hundred forty-three, although some date it to seven hundred ninety. Florescano, by contrast, sees a scene of conquest. None of this is settled. What is certain is that the building holds dates and signs of time. Look at the reliefs and decide what you see, knowing that specialists still debate it.

guion_largo.texto:
A building can tell of an event in the sky. That is what some specialists propose about this pyramid.

The west façade, according to the INAH guide, has an image related to the adjustment of the calendar, and also the name and rank of a ruler. Medina Romero places the calendar correction on the northwest panel, with a date accompanied by two hands.

Hirth also mentions a possible adjustment between two calendar systems. One counts two hundred sixty days and the other, three hundred sixty-five. Since they do not coincide, from time to time they had to be corrected.

There is also a relief with a jaw about to swallow a circle divided into four. According to the INAH guide, it contains a reference to an eclipse of the Sun in the year seven hundred forty-three. Medina Romero reads it as the Moon covering the Sun. That reading is an interpretation.

The proposed dates do not coincide. Medina Romero mentions July twenty-fifth, seven hundred forty-three, with a partial eclipse. The UNAM proposes July sixteenth, seven hundred ninety, closer to a total one. The INAH guide speaks of a total eclipse. Other INAH notes point out internal discrepancies, and Florescano proposes that the relief tells of a conquest, not an eclipse.

Helmke and Nielsen explain that the sign nine Reptile Eye appears twice on the north, east and south sides. They read it as nine Reed, and it is crowned by burning braziers. It could refer to new fire rituals. On the west façade there is also a year nine House. These readings are preliminary, because the writing of Xochicalco has not yet been deciphered.

For decades it was read that the panels were a list of towns that paid tribute to Xochicalco, from Coyoacán to Iguala, according to Hirth. Nielsen and Helmke propose another reading. The upper panels show a row of seated figures with the same headdress and the same title, which they compare to that of the heart devourer of Cacaxtla. They could be people of high rank.

What matters is what we do know. The builders of this city left, on their most carefully made building, signs that have to do with the sky and with time. What exactly they say and what date they mark is still under discussion.

texto: Look on the west façade for the image of the calendar adjustment
Identify the jaw and the circle divided into four
Decide whether you see an eclipse or a scene of conquest

texto.West façade: calendar adjustment and name and rank of the ruler, according to the INAH
texto.Alternative reading: scene of conquest, according to Florescano

texto.pregunta: Myth: It is known for certain that the relief shows an eclipse.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is an interpretation. Other specialists propose a scene of conquest, and the proposed dates do not coincide.
